title: Lecture 2b – Pituitary insufficiency & diabetes insipidus
html:
Source: CursII_MGE IH 2023.pptx – 25 slides

LECTURE II #1

PITUITARY INSUFFICIENCY #2

  • Hypopituitarism is manifested by diminished or absent secretion of one or more pituitary hormones (partial or complete deficiency).
  • Hypopituitarism
  • -either a primary event caused by destruction of the anterior pituitary gland (⇒ deficiency of pituitary trophic hormones) or
  • - a secondary phenomenon resulting from deficiency of hypothalamic stimulatory factors normally acting on the pituitary.
  • Panhypopituitarism refers to deficiency of all anterior pituitary hormones

Etiology of pituitary failure #3

  • A.
  • HYPOTHALAMIC DISORDERS ( deficiency of HPT stimulatory factors normally acting on the pituitary)
  • !!!!!! „Nine Is”
  • B. PITUITARY DISORDERS
  • 1.INVASIVE : Space-occupying lesions: large pituitary adenoma, craniopharyngioma, meningioma, metastasis (e.g., breast, lung). cause hypopituitarism by destroying the pituitary gland or hypothalamic nuclei or by disrupting the hypothalamic-hypophyseal portal venous system.
  • 2. INFARCTION:
  • - ischemic pituitary necrosis: SHEEHAN sdr,
  • - spontaneous hemorrhagic infarction of a pituitary tumor (pituitary apoplexy)
  • -
  • *PITUITARY APOPLEXY
  • *SHEEHAN’S SYNDROME

Slide 4 #4

  • 3. Infiltration – lymphoma, leukaemia, histiocytosis X, hemochromatosis hpt/hpf, sarcoidosis
  • 4. Infectious – tuberculosis, siphilis, mycotic infections,
  • 5.Immunologic – Lymphocytic hypophysitis
  • 6. INJURY : severe head trauma (associated with subarachnoid hemorrhage and skull base fractures; most common deficiencies—GH and gonadotropins (10–15%))
  • 7. Iatrogenic – both surgical and radiation to the pituitary gland may compromise its function
  • 8. Inherited (/congenital/genetic)
  • eg,isolated GH deficiency: congenital monotropic GH deficiency (sporadic or familial) ←mutations within GH and GHRH receptor genes
  • Isolated gonadotropin deficiency:Kallmann sdr ← mutations in the KAL1 gene (isolated defect in GnRH secretion + maldevelopment of the olfactory center with hyposmia or anosmia);
  • OR
  • multiple hormone deficiency ← abnormalities of the genes encoding the transcription factors responsible for the development of the anterior pituitary: Pit-1 (POU1F1) (TSH, GH and PRL) and PROP-1 (TSH, GH, PRL, LH, FSH and ACTH)
  • 9. IDIOPATHIC

Clinical features #5

  • -depend on the type and degree of the hormonal deficits, and the rate of its development.
  • In the majority of cases, the development of (acquired) hypopituitarism follows a characteristic order, with the secretion of GH, then gonadotropins being affected first, followed by TSH and ACTH secretion at a later stage
  • PRL deficiency is rare, except in Sheehan’s syndrome when it represents the initial clinical presentation, manifested by failure of postpartum lactation (actually, the only symptom of PRL deficiency).
  • Hyperprolactinaemia, rather than prolactin deficiency, occurs relatively early because of loss of tonic inhibitory control by dopamine.

Clinical features #6

  • !!! ADH deficiency is virtually unheard of with pituitary adenomas but may be seen rarely with infiltrative disorders and trauma.
  • !!!!!!!!!!!The majority of the clinical features are similar to those occurring when there is target gland insufficiency.

CLINICAL PRESENTATION of pituitary failure #7

  • 1. GH deficiency
  • causes decreased growth in children but may be clinically occult in adult patients. GH deficiency is associated with fatigue, reduced exercise ability, a decreased sense of well-being and a lower health-related quality of life. Decreased muscle mass and increased fat mass (especially abdominal and visceral), low bone mass (osteoporosis), dry wrinkly skin can also be seen; atherosclerosis low cardiac output, hyperlipidemia, and insulin resistance are other consequences of untreated GH insufficiency.
  • 2. GONADOTROPIN deficiency ♀
  • Secondary amenorrhea
  • Loss of axillae and pubic hair
  • Breast atrophy
  • Decreased vaginal lubrication (dyspareunia)
  • Uterine atrophy
  • ♂: decreased libido or erectile dysfunction, loss of the pubic and body hair, testes atrophy in men.
  • 3. THYROTROPIN deficiency – insidious onset
  • fatigue, apathy
  • Non-pitting edema (eg eyelids, hands, feet)
  • Cold intolerance, dry, pale skin
  • diurnal sleepiness
  • constipation
  • bradycardia
  • mentall dullness
  • hoarseness
  • no goiter!

4. CORTICOTROPHIN deficiency ( “white” Addison ) #8

  • Weakness, ! Depigmentation and ↓ tanning ( ← ACTH insufficiency)
  • Arterial hypotension
  • Hypoglycemia
  • Gastrointestinal symptoms :nausea, vomiting, weight loss
  • 5. Hypothalamic disorders
  • Hypothalamic or pineal tumors and primary central nervous system tumors involving the hypothalamus have variable presentations in both children and adults.
  • Thus, besides various degrees of hypopituitarism, the presentation is with headache, visual loss, symptoms of increased intracranial pressure, growth failure, diabetes insipidus or hyperprolactinemia (with galactorrhea) either by hypothalamic injury or by damage to the pituitary stalk.
  • Hypothalamic tumors in childhood may present with precocious puberty

Investigations of hypopituitarism #9

  • The aims:
  • to biochemically confirm and assess the extent of pituitary hormone deficiency and also
  • to elucidate the cause.
  • a. Basal hormone levels
  • Basal concentrations of the anterior pituitary hormone, as well as the target organ hormone, should be measured, as the pituitary hormones may remain within the normal range despite low (↓) levels of target hormone.
  • Measurement of the pituitary hormone alone does not demonstrate that the level is inappropriately low, and the diagnosis may be missed.
  • • (gonadotroph function) LH and FSH, and testosterone (9 a.m.) or oestradiol.
  • • (thyrotroph function) TSH and thyroxine.
  • • (corticotroph function) 8-9 a.m. cortisol.± ACTH
  • • (lactotroph function) PRL.
  • •(somatotroph function) IGF-1± GH
  • In the clinical setting of endocrine hypofunction, basal determinations of each anterior pituitary hormone coupled to target gland secretion are also useful to distinguish pituitary hormone deficiencies from primary failure of the thyroid, adrenals, or gonads.
  • In primary target gland hypofunction, TSH, LH, FSH, or ACTH will be elevated (↑).
  • Low or normal values (↓/N) for these pituitary hormones suggest hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.

b. STIMULATION TESTS #10

  • Provocative endocrine testing may be employed to confirm the diagnosis and to
  • Provocative endocrine testing may then be employed to confirm the diagnosis and to assess the extent of hypofunction. (→the response of an endocrine axis to a specific challenge)
  • ● utility : in partial/ mild pituitary insufficiency (for example low-normal TSH and low FT4)
  • ● assessed with hypothalamic hormones (“liberine”) (releasing hormone tests were a traditional part of pituitary function testing but have been largely replaced by the advent of more reliable assays for basal hormones)
  • ─ for TSH secretory reserve →TRH test
  • ─ for LH and FSH secretory reserves →GnRH test ( use synthetic GnRH (gonadorelin))
  • Do FSH, LH at 0’ and 30’ after adm. of 100ug of GnRH iv.
  • Normally → LH ↑ 4-5 * basal levels while FSH ↑2* basal values
  • ─ for GH and ACTH secretory reserve : Insulin hypoglycemia test (ITT) : the test involves giving insulin IV (0,1-0,2 unit/kg )and assessing its effect on GH and cortisol; Glucose must fall <40mg/dl and the patient should become symptomatic for adequate stimulation;
  • Normal values are: GH : 60’ after insulin adm >7 ng/ml (in children) and a peak cortisol : 30’,60’ >=550nmol/l
  • for ACTH reserve : short Synacthen test provides sufficient information concerning ACTH deficiency: do plasma cortisol before and 30’ after Synacthen 250 µg IV or IM; exclude CSRI if plasma cortisol at 30’ >20 µg/dl (550 nmol/l) (=an indirect measure of HPA status)

c. Other laboratory findings #11

  • These may include anemia (related to thyroid and androgen deficiency and chronic disease), hypoglycemia, hyponatremia (related to hypothyroidism and hypoadrenalism, which cause inappropriate water retention, not sodium loss).
  • d. Investigation of the cause
  • Accurate neuroradiologic assessment of the hypothalamus and pituitary and neuro-ophthalmologic evaluation, which should include pituitary MRI, perimetry, and ophthalmoscopy are essential in confirming the existence and defining the extent of the hypothalamic-pituitary lesion.

Treatment of pituitary insufficiency #12

  • involves :
  • adequate and appropriate hormone replacement
  • management of the underlying cause
  • A. Anterior pituitary hormone replacement
  • THERAPEUTICAL PRINCIPLES
  • √ The correction of the pituitary hormone deficits should be started conversely to their classic course of onset
  • √ Treatment for ACTH and TSH deficits are for life
  • It is managed with the hormones of target gland (The exceptions to this are GH replacement (performed with human recombinant GH) and when fertility is desired.

Slide 13 #13

  • 1.ACTH deficiency –must include glucocorticoid support; mineralocorticoid therapy is not usually required
  • HIDROCORTISONE (15-25 mg/day) or PREDNISONE 5mg/tb (5-7,5 mg/day orally) in 2-3 divided doses
  • Increased dosage is required during periods of stress such as illness, surgery, or trauma.
  • Monitoring of replacement
  • This is important to avoid over-replacement which is associated with features of iatrogenic hypercortisolism. Under-replacement leads to the non-specific symptoms, as seen in Addison’s disease.
  • The clinical assessment is the most important, (but biochemical monitoring, using plasma and urine cortisol (UFC) measurements, is used by some endocrinologists, (but not widely accepted))
  • 2.TSH deficiency
  • LEVOTHYROXINE 50-150 μg/day (1,6μg/kg/day)
  • Note: The adrenal disorder should be treated first, because thyroid hormone replacement may aggravate even partial adrenal insufficiency.
  • Monitoring of therapy
  • In contrast to replacement in primary hypothyroidism, the measurement of TSH cannot be used to assess the adequacy of replacement in TSH deficiency.
  • ⇒ should be via both clinical assessment and by measuring free T4 concentrations, which should be in the middle/upper part of the normal range.

3. FSH, LH deficiency #14

  • Estrogen/testosterone administration is the usual method of replacement, but gonadotrophin therapy is required if fertility is desired.
  • ♀– estrogen and progesterone replacement is essential (→ withdrawal bleeding )
  • several estrogen preparations are available
  • (e.g., oral estradiol 1-2 mg daily;
  • conjugated estrogens 0.3-1.25 mg orally daily or
  • estradiol transdermal(TD) patch=PREFERRED!!! e.g. Vivelle Dot, Estraderm) 0.05-0.1 mg daily)
  • for 21 days.
  • Estrogens should be cycled with a progestin compound (e.g., Dydrogesterone (Duphaston) 10-20 mg daily or Micronised progesterone (e.g. Utrogestan 100-200 mg/day) during the last 10-12 days of estrogen therapy each month) to induce withdrawal bleeding and prevent endometrial hyperplasia.
  • Many oral contraceptive pill combinations are also clinically available.
  • ♂– testosterone replacement therapy;
  • Therapeutic preparations include:
  • Testosterone enanthate, cypionate or mixture of T esters 100-200mg every 2 weeks (adult dose=150–250 mg every 2–4 weeks), IM;
  • Testosterone undecanoate (Nebido) 1000mg IM every 10–14 weeks
  • Transdermal: testosterone patches (non-scrotal) (in doses of 2.5 or 5 mg): daily application
  • Testosterone gels are available in packets and metered-dose pumps: daily

Fertility restoration #15

  • Ovulation induction: Ovulation can often be restored in women with hypothalamic-pituitary dysfunction.
  • In patients with gonadal failure of hypothalamic origin, clomiphene citrate or pulsatile subcutaneous injections of GnRH with an infusion pump can be used to induce ovulation and fertility.
  • Combined treatment with FSH (human menopausal gonadotropins; menotropins) and LH (chorionic gonadotropin) can be utilized to provoke ovulation in women with intrinsic pituitary failure.
  • Spermatogenesis: Spermatogenesis can be achieved in many patients with the combined use of hCG and recombinant FSH. Pulsatile GnRH infusion pumps have also been used to restore fertility in male patients with secondary hypogonadism.
  • 4. GH deficiency
  • In adults, GH is administered subcutaneously, once per day in a dosage of 2 to 5 µg/kg. Monitoring of effectiveness is accomplished by measurement of IGF-I, and the dosage of GH is adjusted accordingly (up to about 10 µg/kg /d).
  • Side effects: edema, paresthesias, arrhythmias, glucose intolerance, diabetes.
  • Contraindications to GH therapy: diabetic retinopathy, active malignancy, intracranial hypertension, or airway obstruction in individuals with Prader-Willi syndrome.

SHORT STATURE #16

  • Definition: Short stature is defined as height 2 SD or more below the mean height for individuals of the same sex and chronologic age in a given population (this translates to a height that is below the 2.3rd percentile).
  • Dwarfism – extremely short stature
  • Disproportionate dwarfism
  • Proportionate dwarfism

Assessment #17

  • History and Examination:
  • Assess height (!!! Accurate measurement of length (<2 years) or height (>2 years) is essential)
  • and height velocity over at least 6 months.
  • What are the parental heights? and calculate target height=midparental height (MPH)= (F height+M height +/- 13)/2
  • Observe for dysmorphic features and abnormal body proportions; arm span and upper segment/lower segment (US/LS) ratio are measured
  • Pubertal stage using Tanner’s criteria and is there a family history of short stature or pubertal delay?
  • Assess for the presence and severity of chronic disease. !!! Low weight for height suggests a nutritional diagnosis, GI cause, or other significant systemic diseases.
  • An initial decision must determine whether a child is pathological short or simply distressed because height is not close to the 50th percentile as desired by the patient or the parents and which short children warrant further evaluation and which ones (and their parents) require only reassurance.
  • Height →SDS of height
  • ←Growth charts allow us to understand whether a measurement is normal by comparing it with the normal range of measurements for other children of the same age and sex)
  • Child’ s height measurements will be compared with the best available references/growth charts (the most recent available growth references for the country or specific ethnic population should be used.
  • The results should also be plotted on the growth chart that is appropriate for the child's age and gender (

Slide 18 #18

  • Height above >-2 SD– These children generally do not require further specific evaluation
  • Height below ≤-2 SD – These children have short stature and should undergo a more detailed evaluation especially if abnormal body proportions (suggestive for a form of skeletal dysplasia) or facial and body dysmorphic features are present
  • SD scores (SDS) of height can be calculated using
  • the equation (formula) illustrated in the example
  • Calculation of height SDS Prader et al (1988)
  • Height standard deviation score (HtSDS) = (actual height − average height for children of the same sex and age) ÷ (SD of the heights for children of the same sex and age)
  • HEIGHT ⇒ height SDS

Slide 19 #19

  • the two most common causes of short stature
Table 8. Growth Disorders
ENDOCRINE DWARFISM True precocious puberty Cushing’s syndrome Hypothyroidism (disproportionate dwarfism, US/LS ratio >1) Pseudohypoparathyroidism Disorders of vitamin D metabolism Untreated diabetes mellitus, diabetes insipidus GH deficiency
2. NONENDOCRINE DWARFISM Genetic short stature Constitutional delay in growth and puberty Skeletal dysplasia (e.g. achondroplasia, hypochondroplasia) (the most common type of short-limb disproportionate dwarfism) Dysmorphic syndromes (e.g. Turner’s syndrome, Noonan’s syndrome) Prader-Willi syndrome Chronic illness (including untreated coeliac disease, congenital heart disease, chronic renal failure, inflammatory bowel disease, pulmonary disorders, hematologic disorders).

Investigations of short stature #20

  • → if no historical or physical features lead to an etiology, laboratory examination is performed.
  • Laboratory tests should include FBC, ESR, electrolytes, liver enzymes (rationale: to assess inflammatory diseases, infections, malignancy), folate, tissue transglutaminase antibodies (rationale: to detect malabsorption, celiac disease), thyroid function (TSH, FT4), calcium, phosphate,IGF-I level, karyotype (of particular importance in girls), and urinalysis.
  • Skeletal (Bone) Age: skeletal development is a reflection of physiologic maturation.
  • Bone age is determined by comparing the shapes and stage of fusion of epiphyses or bones on the patient's radiograph with an atlas (e.g., Greulich and Pyle atlas of radiographs of the left hand and wrist) demonstrating normal skeletal maturation for various ages.

Slide 21 #21

  • Pituitary dwarfism (GH deficiency in children)
  • Etiology
  • Growth hormone deficiency is relatively rare. About one in 4,000 to 6,000 children have GHD
  • Isolated/ Combined with other pituitary hormone deficiencies
Table Growth disturbances due to disorders of GH release or action
Site of defectClinical condition
HypothalamusIdiopathic GH deficiency due to decreased GHRH secretion; hypothalamic tumors or congenital defects.
Pituitary glandSellar and parasellar tumors (eg, craniopharyngioma) or trauma, surgery Pituitary dysplasia, congenital absence of the pituitary gland/ Defect in GH gene or pituitary transcription factors (Pit-1, Prop-1) causing impaired GH biosynthesis
GH receptor: (IGF-1 production )Primary IGF-1 deficiency: GH receptor defect (→Laron dwarfism with ↑ GH and ↓ IGF-1 concentrations

FEATURES #22

  • Clinical presentation
  • Typical features include slow growth velocity, short stature (proportionate short stature (upper/lower segment (US/LS) ratios=almost 1)), ↓ muscle mass and ↑subcutaneous fat.
  • Immature facial appearance, immature high-pitched voice, delayed dental eruption, and delayed closure of the anterior fontanelle, may be seen.
  • These children have delayed bone age and delayed puberty.
  • In infancy, GH deficiency may present with hypoglycemia. Intelligence is normal.
  • Males with GH deficiency may have micropenis (penis< 2 cm at birth), especially if the condition is accompanied by GnRH deficiency, when cryptorchidism may also be noted.
  • Coexisting ACTH and TSH deficiencies may cause prolonged hyperbilirubinemia, more pronounced hypoglycemia, and other features of central hypothyroidism.
  • PITUITARY DEFICIENCY IN CHIDREN (GH deficit-Pituitary “dwarfism”)

DIAGNOSIS OF GH deficiency #23

  • !!!!! Height SDS< -2 SD and especially severe short stature (<-2.5 SD)- deserve investigations
  • 1.!!!! All other causes of decreased growth (hypothyroidism, celiac disease, Turner...) must be considered and ruled out ......before testing the GH-IGF-1 axis
  • 2. Check: IGF-1 (↓)
  • An IGF-1 level should be measured in the baseline sample, as an additional marker of GH status.
  • (→may provide evidence of GH undersecretion.)
  • 3. Because basal values of serum GH are low in normal and GH-deficient patients alike(!!! ↓Basal GH- is not diagnostic for GH deficiency) , ⇒ diagnosis of GH deficiency rests upon demonstration of an inadequate rise of serum GH after provocative stimuli
  • ITT (hypoglycemia induced by IV insulin) - gold standard test to establish the diagnosis using a peak GH cut-point of 10 mcg/l or 7 mcg/l
  • Alternative tests: clonidine, arginine + GHRH and glucagon
  • However, since 10% or more of healthy children do not have an adequate rise in GH with one test of GH reserve at least two methods of assessing GH reserve are necessary before the diagnosis of classic GH deficiency is assigned.
  • For example, the inability of GH to rise above 7 (10) ng/ml in response to hypoglycemia induced by IV insulin (ITT) and to clonidine (0.1 mg/m2 orally) is diagnostic of GH deficiency.
  • 4. Radiographs of the left hand and wrist ( bone age)→ delayed bone age

Treatment #24

  • - replacement therapy with human GH produced by recombinant DNA technology, available since 1985 and administered by daily SC injection.
  • The replacement dose for childhood GH deficiency is 25–75 micrograms/kg/day.
  • Catch-up growth is optimized if GH is commenced early.
  • A higher dose can be used in puberty, reflecting the normal elevation in GH levels at Tanner stage 3–4.
  • Human biosynthetic somatropin (natural sequence GH) (GENOTROPIN®, NORDITROPIN®): once daily, 25-75 mcg/kg/day
  • Somatrogon, a Long-Acting Human Growth Hormone: once-weekly in pre-pubertal children with GHD
  • Side effects of rhGH replacement therapy in children and adolescents include: prepubertal gynecomastia, arthralgia, edema, benign intracranial hypertension, insulin resistance and slipped capital femoral epiphysis.
  • Development of neoplasms is a concern (counseling that should include information about the unknown long-term (i.e., posttreatment) risks of neoplasia still being studied, should be provided).
  • !!!!! Sexual hormone replacement for coexisting gonadotropin deficiency may be started after the target height is reached; otherwise, steroid replacement may advance bone age and lead to epiphyseal fusion and a decrease in ultimate stature!!!
